title: Financial services: HSBC winds down retail banking
full_text:
HSBC says it will wind down its Australian retail banking business after selling a $36 billion book of home and personal loans to private equity giant Blackstone in one of the largest ever mortgage portfolio transactions.
The transaction, first flagged by The Australian Financial Review's Street Talk column earlier this week, marks the end of a four-decade retail banking presence in Australia for the London-headquartered financial giant.
HSBC has held a local banking licence since 1986 when then treasurer Paul Keating opened the market to foreign competitors. Despite its long-term operations, HSBC failed to win substantial market share against the major local banks and flagged an intention to leave more than a year ago.
The bank intends to wind down the remainder of its retail business over the next 18 months, but will retain a presence in corporate and private banking.
"For now, customers can continue to bank with us as normal and will receive information from HSBC outlining the subsequent changes to the products held, noting there is no action required at this point," the company said in a statement on Friday. "HSBC is focused on increasing leadership and market share in the areas where it has clear competitive advantage and the greatest opportunities to grow and support its clients."
HSBC, which was being advised by Citi, had earlier tried to sell its entire retail banking operations including a deposit book of about $19 billion. Before HSBC shelved those plans, Macquarie and National Australia Bank, which acquired Citi's retail operations for $1.2 billion in 2021, were widely expected to be the frontrunners to pick up the entire division.
The bank's review of its local operations came after the promotion of George Elhedery to chief executive in late 2024. Elhedery, who beat now ANZ chief executive Nuno Matos to the top job, almost immediately embarked on a major restructuring, closing parts of its investment banking division. Earlier this month it agreed to sell its Singapore insurance business to German giant Allianz for $US2.1 billion ($3 billion).
The sale is the latest in a string of loan book transactions, the most significant of which was the acquisition of the $21.4 billion RAMS Home Loans portfolio, or about 1 per cent of the mortgages market, by a consortium that included Pepper Money, KKR and PIMCO. Pepper Money, which is listed on the ASX with a market capitalisation of $786 million but is majority-owned by KKR, will act as the servicer of the HSBC home and personal loan portfolio on Blackstone's behalf.
The transaction could be emulated by other Australian banks that are considering ways to release capital. Earlier this week, MST Financial analyst Lafitani Sotiriou speculated that AMP's banking unit might consider a sale of its home loan book to unlock capital within the broader group.
Blackstone was advised by Morgan Stanley and Barrenjoey. The transaction broadens its presence in Australia after a series of high-profile transactions, which included its purchase of data centre operator AirTrunk from Macquarie Asset Management and PSP Investments for $23.5 billion in 2024. The New York-listed investment manager last year acquired Hamilton Island from the Oatley family and has owned casino and hotel operator Crown Resorts since 2022.
The HSBC loans will be housed in three Blackstone funds - credit and insurance, tactical opportunities and real estate debt - and is part of a push among private asset managers to engage in asset-backed finance.
"International expansion is a major priority for our private credit business," said Dan Leiter, who heads international investing for Blackstone Credit & Insurance. "This marquee investment is a testament to the power of our franchise and our conviction in the growing opportunities in credit."
